chapters.c: The author introduces the book as answers he used to give in private conversations, now written down so everyone can have them. He asks readers to study it carefully, and to bring hard questions to the scholars of their town rather than to him.

The book opens with a puzzle: before birth each soul is told “be righteous” yet also “regard yourself as wicked.” To answer it, the chapter sets out five types of people (the righteous, the wicked and the benoni in between) and introduces the idea that every Jew has two souls. The first, the animal soul, is described here.

The second soul is “truly a part of God above.” Using the image of a child who comes from the father’s mind, the chapter explains how every soul, great or simple, stays connected to its source. The link is strengthened or weakened by how a person lives.

The Godly soul has ten faculties that mirror the ten sefirot: three of intellect (chochmah, binah, daat) and seven of emotion, headed by love and awe. Understanding produces feeling: contemplating God’s greatness gives birth to love and fear of Him.

The soul expresses itself through three “garments”: thought, speech and action. When they are used for Torah study and mitzvot, the soul is clothed in God’s own will and wisdom, and so is united with Him in a way that nothing else allows.

A close look at what it means to “grasp” an idea. When you understand a law of the Torah, your mind holds God’s wisdom and is held by it. That is why studying Torah is the most complete union with God.

Opposite the holy soul stands a soul drawn from the sitra achara, “the other side.” It has its own ten faculties and three garments. Every thought, word and act that is not for God’s sake feeds this side.

chapters.h: Things that can be lifted up
chapters.c: Permitted things, including food and the animal soul’s own energy, come from kelipat nogah, a mix of good and bad. They can be raised to holiness when used for a Godly purpose, or dragged down when used purely for indulgence.
Forbidden things are bound (“chained”) and cannot be elevated. The chapter also warns about idle talk and secular study used for its own sake, and explains how both weigh on the soul.

chapters.h: The battle for the small city
chapters.c: The animal soul lives in the left side of the heart and the Godly soul in the brain and right side of the heart. The body is a “small city” that both want to rule. Each soul wants to be the only one that fills it.
A tzaddik is someone who has overcome the evil within. A complete tzaddik has turned it entirely to good, while an incomplete one still has a trace left. There are countless levels within these two.
The mirror image of the tzaddik: someone in whom the animal soul sometimes wins and leads the body to sin. This too has many levels. Even so, the Godly soul never truly leaves; it hovers over them.
The central definition of the book. A benoni still feels desire, but evil never gets to act. They never sin in thought, speech or deed, because the mind rules the heart at every moment of choice.

Why the benoni still feels like an inbetweener: the animal soul keeps its full strength and only the Godly soul’s control keeps it from acting. So the benoni truly sees themself as “not yet there,” which resolves the puzzle from chapter one.

Being a tzaddik depends on a heart that many people are not given. Being a benoni depends on choices anyone can make. So this is the level to aim for, and a person can live as a benoni at any given hour.

The difference between “one who serves God” and “one who does not serve Him” is effort. Whoever is still fighting their nature, or going beyond their habits, is serving; doing only what comes easily does not count as the same service.

The practical rule for the benoni: use the mind to govern the heart. Even when contemplation does not produce strong feeling, the understanding it produces is enough to drive real action, and that action counts.

The Torah says keeping it is “very near… in your mouth and in your heart.” Changing the heart is hard, but controlling your mouth and hands is always within reach. Doing that also slowly brings the heart along.
Every Jew, even one who knows little, carries an inherited, hidden love for God from the patriarchs. It rests in the soul’s faculty of chochmah, above ordinary reason. That is why it is “very near.”
The soul is compared to a flame that always leaps upward toward its source. That natural pull explains why even ordinary Jews have been ready to give their lives rather than deny God.

The whole Torah is summed up in “I am” and “You shall have no other gods.” The chapter begins explaining God’s absolute unity: before Him, the whole of creation is like a single word compared with the soul that speaks it.
Human speech separates from the speaker; God’s “speech” does not. The words that create the world stay united with Him, so nothing truly exists apart from Him.

If everything is part of God’s word, how can anything seem separate? The answer is contraction (tzimtzum) and concealment. The less of God’s will that shows in something, the more it can feel independent, and that is the root of kelipah.
The mitzvot are God’s inner will, and the Torah is His wisdom. So studying Torah or doing a mitzvah clothes you in God Himself, which is a far deeper union than any ordinary spiritual experience.
The opposite of chapter 23: a forbidden act, even a brief one, separates a person from God’s unity as completely as idolatry would. Seeing this clearly is meant to help a person hold back.

People would give their lives rather than be separated from God for a moment by idolatry. If you remember that any sin separates just the same, you can find that same resolve in ordinary choices, at any moment.

Like a wrestler, you cannot win while sluggish; sadness is the enemy. Worry over worldly things should be dropped, and remorse over sins belongs at set times. After remorse should come true joy that you have been forgiven.
Unwanted thoughts are no reason for sadness. Each time a benoni pushes one away, they give God real pleasure, and this struggle is exactly what they were created for.
Stray thoughts during prayer or study are not a sign that the prayer is worthless. Do not argue with them; ignore them and keep going. They come because of the battle between two souls.
Sometimes the heart simply will not open. The advice: humble the animal soul by reflecting honestly on its coarseness, and remember that the struggle itself counts.

“Do not judge your fellow until you have stood in their place.” A person should see themself as lower than others, since others may face harder trials. The chapter also gives a demanding standard for measuring one’s own shortcomings.
Reflecting on your failings can produce a broken heart. This bitterness is healthy, unlike sadness. It should be followed by joy in the soul’s true nature and in the chance to bring it home.

If you value the soul above the body, loving every Jew becomes easy, since all souls share one source. The chapter also covers how to treat someone who does wrong: rebuke with love, and hate only the wrongdoing.
Meditating on God’s unity, that He fills and surrounds all worlds and nothing exists apart from Him, is a source of lasting joy. It is also the core of faith.
The patriarchs were a “chariot” for God. Every person can be a dwelling for Him in a smaller way, through Torah study and mitzvot, and should be glad of that portion even while feeling humble.

Why would a soul come into a body it will never fully master? This chapter starts the answer. Through mitzvot done with the body, God’s light rests in the physical world itself, and the image used is a candle and its oil.

chapters.h: A home in the lower world
chapters.c: God wanted “a dwelling place in the lowest realm.” This world, the most concealed, is where revealing Him matters most. That revelation will be complete in the era of Mashiach.
The Messianic revelation depends on our deeds now. Each mitzvah refines the world and adds light, and charity is singled out because it involves the whole of a person’s effort.
Why actually speaking and acting matter more than intention alone, and why intention (kavanah) still matters. Kavanah is the soul of the mitzvah, and the act is its body.
Service with love and awe rises to the higher worlds, and service without them stays below. The chapter compares the service of angels and souls and the different levels that intention can reach.
Learning with love or awe raises Torah study to the sefirot, and learning without them keeps it lower. Even so, study done without the right intention is never lost: it waits to be lifted later.
Before anything else, stand before the King. Remember that God stands over you and sees everything. That simple awe is the foundation, and even a little of it is enough to begin.
“What does God ask of you but to fear Him?” Awe is within reach for everyone once they train their mind to picture that God is present and sees them, with the same clarity as physical sight.
Two kinds of awe (practical fear of doing wrong, and awe at God’s greatness) and two kinds of love. Awe is the first step, and love is the goal.
Each kind of love has countless shades, and each person reaches God according to their own capacity. Hidden love must be brought out and turned into action.
Another road to love: feel compassion for your own soul, a spark of God far from home. That compassion, Jacob’s trait, opens the way to great love.
“As water reflects a face, so the heart of one person answers another.” Reflecting on how much God loves us naturally awakens love in return.
Every day a person should feel they have just left Egypt: freed from the body’s limits into God’s unity, especially when saying the Shema.
God’s light is infinite; a finite world needs a contraction of it. Understanding that He shrank Himself for us, out of love, is itself a reason for love.
The descent from God’s light to our world passes through three great contractions, which produce the worlds. Seeing how far He came down for us awakens the wish to give ourselves to Him in return.
Beyond the “silver” love of kindness there is a “golden” love like fire: a burning desire to leave everything and cling to God. It comes from the side of gevurah.
If God fills the world, what does it mean that the Shechinah “dwells” somewhere? The answer uses the soul and body: life is everywhere in the body, but it is revealed most in the brain.
In the same way, God’s life-force reaches all worlds, but it is revealed mostly through malchut, His “word,” also called Shechinah. It is what gives all creatures life.
In the First Temple, God’s Presence rested in the Ark. Today a person studying Torah or doing mitzvot becomes that place, drawing the Shechinah into the world. Part One ends here.

glossary.benoni: The “inbetweener”: someone who still feels the pull of desire but never lets it win in thought, speech or action. The book’s central figure.
glossary.benonim: Plural of benoni. People who still feel desire but never act on it.
glossary.tzaddik: A righteous person: someone who has overcome the evil within, not just its expression.
glossary.en sof: “Without end”: the Infinite. The name used for God as He is beyond any limit or description.
glossary.sitra achara: “The other side”: everything that conceals God and acts as if it were separate from Him.
glossary.kelipah: “Shell” or “husk”: a force that covers holiness the way a peel covers fruit. The source of selfishness and evil.
glossary.kelipot: Plural of kelipah: the “shells” that conceal holiness.
glossary.kelipat nogah: The “glowing shell”: a mix of good and bad. Permitted things come from it and can be raised to holiness.
glossary.nogah: Short for kelipat nogah: the mixed realm that can be raised to holiness.
glossary.shechinah: God’s indwelling Presence, as it is revealed within the world.
glossary.sefirot: The ten Divine attributes through which God relates to creation, such as wisdom, understanding, kindness and strength.
glossary.ten sefirot: The ten Divine attributes through which God relates to creation.
glossary.chochmah: Wisdom: the first flash of insight, before it is worked out.
glossary.binah: Understanding: developing an insight in depth and detail.
glossary.daat: Knowledge: deep, sustained focus that turns understanding into real feeling.
glossary.chabad: An acronym of chochmah, binah and daat, the three intellectual powers. It is also the name of the movement founded by the author.
glossary.middot: The emotional attributes, such as love, awe and compassion.
glossary.gevurah: Strength or restraint: the attribute of discipline and awe.
glossary.gevurot: Plural of gevurah: forces of restraint.
glossary.chasadim: Plural of chesed: acts or forces of kindness.
glossary.tiferet: Beauty or harmony: the balance of kindness and restraint, and the source of compassion.
glossary.malchut: Kingship: the last sefirah, through which God’s will reaches and rules creation.
glossary.nefesh: Soul, or specifically the lowest level of the soul, which gives life to the body.
glossary.ruach: Spirit: the middle level of the soul, tied to the emotions.
glossary.neshamah: The higher soul, tied to the intellect.
glossary.atzilut: The World of Emanation: the highest of the four worlds, where nothing yet feels separate from God.
glossary.beriah: The World of Creation: the first world where created beings feel separate from God.
glossary.yetzirah: The World of Formation: the realm of angels and emotions.
glossary.asiyah: The World of Action: the lowest world, which includes our physical one.
glossary.tzimtzum: Contraction: God limiting and hiding His infinite light so that a finite world can exist.
glossary.tzimtzumim: Plural of tzimtzum: stages of contraction.
glossary.hishtalshelut: The chain of worlds: the step-by-step descent from God’s light to our world.
glossary.kavanah: Intention or focus, especially in prayer and mitzvot.
glossary.yirah tataah: Lower awe: fear of disobeying God, which keeps a person from wrongdoing.
glossary.yirah ilaah: Higher awe: awe at God’s greatness.
glossary.ahavah rabbah: “Great love”: an overwhelming love for God, understood as a gift from above.
glossary.ahavat olam: “Eternal love”: love for God that grows from contemplating His greatness.
glossary.shema: The declaration “Hear O Israel… God is One,” said morning and evening.
glossary.etz chaim: “Tree of Life”: the main work of the Arizal’s Kabbalah, written down by Rabbi Chaim Vital.
glossary.atzvut: Sadness or dejection, which the Tanya treats as a real obstacle to serving God.
glossary.yichud: Union, especially the union of the soul, or the worlds, with God.
glossary.pardes: The four levels of Torah interpretation: plain meaning, hint, homily and mystical secret.
glossary.chayot: A class of angels whose awe and love of God are instinctive.

parts.name: Likkutei Amarim
parts.label: Chapter
parts.c: The heart of the Tanya: two souls, the benoni, and a practical path of mind over heart.

parts.name: Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah
parts.en: The Gate of Unity and Faith
parts.label: Chapter
parts.c: A study of God’s unity. Creation is brought into being anew at every moment by Divine “speech,” so from God’s point of view nothing exists apart from Him. It opens with a short introduction, Chinuch Katan, that ties the idea to the Shema.

parts.name: Iggeret HaTeshuvah
parts.label: Chapter
parts.c: What teshuvah really is: returning to God by leaving a wrong behind with full resolve. It covers fasting and atonement, and the difference between “lower” and “higher” teshuvah, all with an emphasis on joy.

parts.name: Iggeret HaKodesh
parts.label: Epistle
parts.c: Letters the author sent to his chassidim over many years, collected after his passing. Many are about charity (tzedakah), and others cover prayer, Torah study, love between people and deep Kabbalistic themes.

parts.name: Kuntres Acharon
parts.label: Essay
parts.c: Short essays that clarify difficult points in Part One, especially about Torah study, the mitzvot and intention (kavanah).
